claims.text: Adding 1–5 wt% graphene nanoplatelets to the HEA will produce a lubricious, self-adapting tribofilm during sliding.
The graphene-derived tribofilm will reduce the coefficient of friction relative to the untreated HEA.
The graphene-derived tribofilm will reduce wear rate relative to the untreated HEA.
The friction and wear benefits will persist from room temperature to approximately 600°C.
Powder mixing followed by consolidation such as spark plasma sintering can produce a uniform dispersion of graphene in the HEA.
Sliding will cause the dispersed graphene nanoplatelets to form a continuous or semi-continuous surface layer at the contact interface.
The graphene-rich surface layer will enable easy interfacial shear.
The graphene-rich surface layer will protect the underlying HEA from direct wear.
Graphene's lamellar structure provides low shear strength.
Applied load and frictional heating will cause graphene-rich surface regions to shear easily, thereby reducing friction.
The protective tribofilm will minimize direct metal-to-metal contact and abrasion, thereby lowering wear rate.
Graphene addition may reduce the coefficient of friction by roughly 20–30% relative to the untreated HEA.
The untreated HEA has higher friction and wear rates than the proposed graphene-doped alloy under otherwise identical conditions.
The beneficial effect will remain valid under dry sliding in atmospheres ranging from inert to ambient.
Very high humidity may impair the efficacy of the graphene tribofilm.
Temperatures above approximately 600°C may impair the efficacy of the graphene tribofilm.
Prior analogous systems have shown that two-dimensional materials can reduce friction and wear.
